title: Seeking Refuge in Abyssinia
subtitle: The First Migration, the Christian Negus, and Safe Haven Across the Sea
summary: Escalating persecution in Makkah, the Prophet's advice to seek refuge in Abyssinia, the departure of the first small group of emigrants including 'Uthman and Ruqayyah, the sea crossing from Shu'aybah, the protection of the Negus, and the return of some emigrants to Makkah.

sections.text: The Crisis of Persecution in Makkah

By around the fifth year of the prophetic mission (approx. 615 CE), the hostility of Quraysh had grown into widespread persecution. Even believers from noble clans faced pressure, confinement and ostracism from their own families.

Ibn Ishaq relates that when the Prophet ﷺ saw the affliction falling on his Companions, while he himself was safe through God's protection and that of his uncle Abu Talib, and that he could not protect them, he advised them to leave.
The Prophetic Counsel: The Land of the Just King
He directed them toward the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia (al-Habashah), across the Red Sea in the region of present-day Ethiopia. Ibn Ishaq gives his words as follows:

"If you were to go out to the land of Abyssinia, for there is a king there under whom no one is wronged, and it is a land of truthfulness, until God grants you relief from what you are in." — Ibn Ishaq, in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham; also in Tarikh al-Tabari
The king was known by the title al-Najashi (the Negus); Sahih al-Bukhari gives his name as Ashamah, and sirah works call him Ashamah ibn Abjar. He was a Christian ruler known for his justice.
The ancient stone mountains and highland landscapes of the Kingdom of Aksum in Abyssinia.
The Secret Departure of the First Emigrants

Ibn Sa'd, following al-Waqidi, dates the departure of the first group to Rajab of the fifth year of prophethood and counts eleven men and four women. Ibn Ishaq names ten men, some with their wives, as the first to leave, and other lists differ slightly. Leaving their homes and families was a heavy sacrifice.

Among them were 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ. A report with a weak chain says that the Prophet described them as the first to emigrate for the sake of God with their family since the Prophet Lut (Lot). The group also included 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam, Abu Salamah and his wife Umm Salamah, and 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, whom Ibn Hisham reports some scholars named as their leader.
The Red Sea Crossing at Shu'aybah

According to Ibn Sa'd, the emigrants left Makkah secretly and reached the Red Sea anchorage of Shu'aybah, where they found two merchant ships about to sail. They were taken aboard for half a dinar each.
Ibn Sa'd adds that Quraysh went out after them as far as the sea, but the emigrants had already sailed, and the pursuers caught none of them.
Desert caravans traveling along coastal trade highways toward the Red Sea ports.
A Generous Sanctuary in Aksum
The emigrants crossed the sea safely and settled in Abyssinia, where the Negus allowed them to live in safety and practise their religion, as the Prophet had described.

Umm Salamah later described their stay, in a report preserved in Musnad Ahmad: 'When we came down in the land of Abyssinia, we had there the best of neighbours, the Negus. We were safe in our religion, and we worshipped God without being harmed and without hearing anything we disliked.'
The Prostration at Surah An-Najm and the Return of Some Emigrants

Ibn Ishaq relates that after some time news reached the emigrants that the people of Makkah had accepted Islam, and some of them set out for home. Sahih al-Bukhari records an event that may lie behind such news: when the Prophet recited Surah An-Najm in Makkah, he prostrated at its end, and those present prostrated with him.
"The Prophet ﷺ prostrated at An-Najm, and with him prostrated the Muslims, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind." — Ibn 'Abbas, Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 1071

A later story that tries to explain why the polytheists prostrated, sometimes called the story of the 'cranes' (gharaniq), is disputed, and many scholars reject it as lacking a sound chain; it is not relied on here. When the returning emigrants neared Makkah, Ibn Ishaq relates, they learned that the news was false. Some went back to Abyssinia, while others entered Makkah secretly or under the protection of a Makkan chief; Ibn Sa'd places their return in Shawwal of the same year. Persecution soon grew worse, leading to a second, larger migration to Abyssinia.

The first migration to Abyssinia was a turning point. It showed that the believers were prepared to leave their homeland to preserve their faith, and it established a refuge that would protect Muslims for years to come.
